Borel Local Lemma: arbitrary random variables and
limited exponential growthThanks: AB’s research is partially supported by the NSF CAREER grant DMS-2239187 and the Sloan Research Fellowship (2025). JY’s research is partially supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China grants 12371343 and 12525110 (PI: Hehui Wu).

Anton Bernshteyn Address: (AB) Department of Mathematics, University of California, Los Angeles, CA, USA Email address: bernshteyn@math.ucla.edu and Jing Yu Address: (JY) Shanghai Center for Mathematical Sciences, Fudan University, Shanghai, China Email address: jyu@fudan.edu.cn
Abstract.

The Lovász Local Lemma (the LLL for short) is a powerful tool in probabilistic combinatorics that is used to verify the existence of combinatorial objects with desirable properties. Recent years saw the development of various “constructive” versions of the LLL. A major success of this research direction is the Borel version of the LLL due to Csóka, Grabowski, Máthé, Pikhurko, and Tyros, which holds under a subexponential growth assumption. A drawback of their approach is that it only applies when the underlying random variables take values in a finite set. We present an alternative proof of a Borel version of the LLL that holds even if the underlying random variables are continuous and applies to dependency graphs of limited exponential growth.

1.  Introduction

This paper is a contribution to Borel combinatorics: an area at the crossroads of combinatorics and descriptive set theory that aims to perform combinatorial constructions using Borel sets and functions. For an overview of this subject, see the survey [29] by Kechris and Marks and introductory articles [39] by Pikhurko and [8] by the first named author. We also direct the reader to [32, 45] for a general introduction to descriptive set theory. While most work in Borel combinatorics addresses specific combinatorial problems, a recent trend is to design general tools that can be applied to broad problem classes [6, 7, 9, 10, 11, 17, 21, 22, 40, 46, 4]. One such tool is the Lovász Local Lemma (the LLL for short): a probabilistic statement that, under certain numerical conditions, guarantees the existence of a labeling satisfying a set of constraints [18, 43, 1]. Recent years saw an explosion of “constructive” versions of the LLL, for various notions of “constructiveness” [2, 12, 13, 19, 37, 41, 6, 9, 10, 17, 4]. Here we are interested in the behavior of the LLL in the Borel setting. Specifically, our goal is to generalize and sharpen the Borel LLL for dependency graphs of subexponential growth due to Csóka, Grabowski, Máthé, Pikhurko, and Tyros [17].

There exist several essentially equivalent frameworks for stating the LLL in the Borel context [6, 8, 17]. We shall find the following formalism convenient:

Definition 1.1 (Constraint satisfaction problems).

A constraint satisfaction problem (a CSP for short) is a tuple Π=(V,Λ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆,ℬ)\Pi=(V,\Lambda,\mathfrak{C},\mathsf{dom},\mathcal{B}), where:

  • —

    VV, Λ\Lambda, and ℭ\mathfrak{C} are sets whose elements are called variables, labels, and constraints respectively,

  • —

    𝖽𝗈𝗆\mathsf{dom} assigns to each constraint 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} a finite set 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)⊆V\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\subseteq V called the domain of 𝔠\mathfrak{c},

  • —

    ℬ\mathcal{B} assigns to each constraint 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} a set ℬ⁡(𝔠)⊆Λ𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})\subseteq\Lambda^{\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})} of bad labelings φ:𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)→Λ\varphi\colon\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\to\Lambda.

A function f:V→Λf\colon V\to\Lambda is called a labeling of VV. Such a labeling ff violates a constraint 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} if its restriction to 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c}) is in ℬ⁡(𝔠)\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c}); otherwise, ff satisfies 𝔠\mathfrak{c}. A solution to Π\Pi is a labeling f:V→Λf\colon V\to\Lambda that satisfies every constraint 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}.

Let us illustrate this definition with a couple of simple examples showing how natural combinatorial problems can be represented by CSPs.

Example 1.2 (Proper coloring).

Given a graph GG and a natural number11 1 In this paper, 00 is a natural number, and a natural number kk is identified with the kk-element set {i∈ℕ:i<k}\{i\in{\mathbb{N}}\,:\,i<k\}. k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}, a proper kk-coloring of GG is a function f:V⁡(G)→kf\colon V(G)\to k such that f⁡(u)≠f⁡(v)f(u)\neq f(v) whenever {u,v}∈E⁡(G)\{u,v\}\in E(G). It is clear that a proper kk-coloring of GG is the same as a solution to the CSP

Πk​(G)≔(V⁡(G),k,E⁡(G),𝗂𝖽,ℬ),\Pi_{k}(G)\,\coloneqq\,\big(V(G),\,k,\,E(G),\,\mathsf{id},\,\mathcal{B}\big),

where for each edge e∈E⁡(G)e\in E(G), 𝗂𝖽⁡(e)≔e\mathsf{id}(e)\coloneqq e (i.e., the domain of the corresponding constraint is the set containing the two endpoints of ee), while ℬ⁡(e)\mathcal{B}(e) is the set of all constant mappings φ:e→k\varphi\colon e\to k.

Example 1.3 (Sinkless orientation).

Let GG be a locally finite graph. An orientation of GG is sinkless if it has no sinks, i.e., no vertices with outdegree 00. The problem of finding a sinkless orientation of GG can be encoded by a CSP Π∙⁣→​(G)\Pi_{\bullet\to}(G) as follows. Fix an arbitrary orientation G→0\vec{G}_{0} of GG. We can then identify any orientation G→\vec{G} of GG with a labeling f:E⁡(G)→{+,−}f\colon E(G)\to\{{+},{-}\}, where f(e)=+f(e)={+} if and only if ee is oriented the same in G→\vec{G} and G→0\vec{G}_{0}. Now we let

Π∙⁣→(G)≔(E(G),{+,−},V(G),∂G,ℬ),\Pi_{\bullet\to}(G)\,\coloneqq\,\big(E(G),\,\{{+},{-}\},\,V(G),\,\partial_{G},\,\mathcal{B}\big),

where for each vertex v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), ∂G(v)\partial_{G}(v) is the set of all edges of GG incident to vv and ℬ⁡(v)\mathcal{B}(v) contains the unique mapping φ:∂G(v)→{+,−}\varphi\colon\partial_{G}(v)\to\{{+},{-}\} that makes vv a sink.

The list of examples can be continued almost indefinitely and includes such classical problems as perfect matching, maximal independent set, edge coloring, hypergraph coloring, graph homomorphism, and so on. We remark that in most combinatorial applications, the set of labels Λ\Lambda is finite; however, that is not a requirement in Definition 1.1.

In view of the versatility of Definition 1.1, it is desirable to develop flexible general conditions that guarantee the existence of a solution to a given CSP Π\Pi. The LLL gives just such a condition. Roughly, the LLL says that Π\Pi has a solution provided that: (a) the constraints interact with each other “in a limited way,” and (b) each individual constraint is “unlikely” to be violated.

The interaction between the constraints is captured by the dependency graph of Π\Pi:

Definition 1.4 (Dependency graph).

Let Π=(V,Λ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆,ℬ)\Pi=(V,\Lambda,\mathfrak{C},\mathsf{dom},\mathcal{B}) be a CSP. The dependency graph of Π\Pi, denoted by DΠD_{\Pi}, is the graph with vertex set ℭ\mathfrak{C} and edge set {{𝔠,𝔠′}:𝔠≠𝔠′,𝖽𝗈𝗆(𝔠)∩𝖽𝗈𝗆(𝔠′)≠∅}.\{\{\mathfrak{c},\mathfrak{c}^{\prime}\}\,:\,\mathfrak{c}\neq\mathfrak{c}^{\prime},\,\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\cap\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c}^{\prime})\neq\varnothing\}.

Throughout, we shall assume the dependency graph DΠD_{\Pi} has finite maximum degree. Intuitively, the smaller the maximum degree of DΠD_{\Pi} is, the less the constraints interact with each other.

To measure how likely each constraint is to be violated, we equip the label set Λ\Lambda with a probability measure ℙ\mathbb{P}. To unclutter the notation, we shall, when there is no possibility of confusion, use the symbol “ℙ\mathbb{P}” not only for the given measure on Λ\Lambda but also for product measures of the form ℙS\mathbb{P}^{S} on ΛS\Lambda^{S} for some set SS. Now, for a constraint 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, we can randomly generate a labeling φ:𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)→Λ\varphi\colon\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\to\Lambda (i.e., a point in Λ𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)\Lambda^{\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})}) by drawing the labels φ⁡(v)\varphi(v) for each v∈𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)v\in\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c}) independently from (Λ,ℙ)(\Lambda,\mathbb{P}). The likelihood of violating 𝔠\mathfrak{c} is simply the probability the resulting labeling is bad, i.e., ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔠)]\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})].

With these preliminaries, we are ready to state the Lovász Local Lemma:

Theorem 1.5 (Lovász Local Lemma [18, 43, 1]).

Let Π=(V,Λ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆,ℬ)\Pi=(V,\Lambda,\mathfrak{C},\mathsf{dom},\mathcal{B}) be a CSP and let ℙ\mathbb{P} be a probability measure on Λ\Lambda making (Λ,ℙ)(\Lambda,\mathbb{P}) a standard probability space. If there exist p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1) and d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}} such that:

  • —

    ℬ⁡(𝔠)\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c}) is ℙ\mathbb{P}-measurable and ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔠)]⩽p\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})]\leqslant p for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C},

  • —

    the maximum degree of the dependency graph DΠD_{\Pi} is at most dd, and

  • —

    𝖾​p​(d+1)<1\mathsf{e}\,p\,(d+1)<1 (where 𝖾=2.71​…\mathsf{e}=2.71\ldots is the base of the natural logarithm),

then Π\Pi has a solution f:V→Λf\colon V\to\Lambda.

Remarks 1.6.
  1. (i)

    The above statement of the LLL is somewhat restricted compared to the more standard version typically found in the combinatorics literature, in that we compute the probability ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔠)]\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})] with respect to specifically the product measure on Λ𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)\Lambda^{\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})}. This set-up is sometimes called the variable version of the LLL. Even though this setting is not the most general, it does encompass virtually all standard applications [36, 41] and is often viewed as the “right one” for algorithmic considerations (see, e.g., [2, 37, 19]). That being said, it is possible to formulate the LLL without assuming a product structure on the underlying probability space; see [1, §5.1] for the statement of the LLL in abstract probability spaces and [33, 14, 27] for comparisons between the abstract and variable versions of the LLL.

  2. (ii)

    Although the LLL is usually stated and proved in the case when the set of constraints ℭ\mathfrak{C} is finite, Theorem 1.5 remains valid even if ℭ\mathfrak{C} is infinite. Indeed, we may without loss of generality assume that Λ\Lambda is a compact metric space and ℙ\mathbb{P} is a Borel probability measure [32, Thm. 17.41]. Pick any p′>pp^{\prime}>p such that 𝖾​p′​(d+1)<1\mathsf{e}\,p^{\prime}\,(d+1)<1 and replace each ℬ⁡(𝔠)\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c}) by an open set ℬ′​(𝔠)⊇ℬ⁡(𝔠)\mathcal{B}^{\prime}(\mathfrak{c})\supseteq\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c}) of measure at most p′p^{\prime}, which is possible since ℙ\mathbb{P} is regular [32, Thm. 17.10]. The existence of a solution to Π\Pi now follows by applying the LLL to finite subsets of ℭ\mathfrak{C} and using the compactness of the space ΛV\Lambda^{V}; see, e.g., [1, proof of Thm. 5.2.2] for details.

In this paper we are interested in the following general question:

Question 1.7.

Let Π=(V,Λ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆,ℬ)\Pi=(V,\Lambda,\mathfrak{C},\mathsf{dom},\mathcal{B}) be a CSP such that VV and Λ\Lambda are standard Borel spaces. When can the LLL be invoked to conclude that there exists a Borel solution f:V→Λf\colon V\to\Lambda to Π\Pi?

Recall that a standard Borel space is a set XX equipped with a σ\sigma-algebra 𝔅⁡(X)\mathfrak{B}(X) generated by a complete separable metric on XX. The members of 𝔅⁡(X)\mathfrak{B}(X) are called the Borel subsets of XX. By the Borel Isomorphism Theorem [32, Thm. 15.6], all uncountable standard Borel spaces are isomorphic to each other, so, as a rule, no generality is lost by replacing XX with some familiar space, such as the real line ℝ\mathbb{R}. A function f:X→Yf\colon X\to Y between standard Borel spaces is Borel if ff-preimages of Borel subsets of YY are Borel in XX, or, equivalently, if the graph of ff is a Borel subset of X×YX\times Y [32, Thm. 14.12]. Borel sets and functions have a variety of useful regularity properties and are generally taken to represent the “gold standard” of well-behavedness in descriptive set theory.

Unfortunately, as the next example illustrates, even under very favorable circumstances, the solutions produced by the LLL may fail to be Borel.

Example 1.8 (Borel sinkless orientation—a negative result).

Fix d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}} and let GG be a dd-regular graph (meaning that every vertex of GG has exactly dd neighbors). Recall the sinkless orientation problem Π∙⁣→​(G)\Pi_{\bullet\to}(G) from Example 1.3. It is easy to see that the dependency graph of Π∙⁣→​(G)\Pi_{\bullet\to}(G) is GG itself, hence its maximum degree is dd. Letting ℙ\mathbb{P} be the uniform probability distribution on {+,−}\{+,-\}, we have ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(v)]=2−d≕p\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(v)]=2^{-d}\eqqcolon p for each v∈V⁡(G)v\in V(G), because exactly one out of the 2d2^{d} ways to orient the edges incident to vv is bad. The inequality

𝖾​p​(d+1)=𝖾​ 2−d​(d+1)< 1\mathsf{e}\,p\,(d+1)\,=\,\mathsf{e}\,2^{-d}\,(d+1)\,<\,1

is satisfied for all d⩾4d\geqslant 4; moreover, its left-hand side rapidly approaches 00 as dd goes to infinity. Nevertheless, no matter how large dd is, GG may fail to have a Borel sinkless orientation, since Thornton [44, Thm. 3.5], using the determinacy method of Marks [35], constructed for each d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}} a Borel dd-regular graph GG with no Borel sinkless orientation.

While the above example shows the LLL may fail to produce a Borel solution in general, there has been a recent string of positive “LLL-like” results in descriptive set theory [6, 8, 17, 4, 10]. Most of these results yield weaker conclusions (e.g., measurable in place of Borel) or require stronger bounds than 𝖾​p​(d+1)<1\mathsf{e}\,p\,(d+1)<1 (often both). A notable exception is the Borel version of the LLL due to Csóka, Grabowski, Máthé, Pikhurko, and Tyros [17]. Their result yields a Borel solution to a given CSP Π\Pi under the usual LLL condition 𝖾​p​(d+1)<1\mathsf{e}\,p\,(d+1)<1; to achieve this, they add some extra assumptions on Π\Pi, the main one being that the dependency graph DΠD_{\Pi} ought to be of subexponential growth.

Definition 1.9 (Growth of graphs).

The growth function γG:ℕ→ℕ∪{∞}\gamma_{G}\colon{\mathbb{N}}\to{\mathbb{N}}\cup\{\infty\} of a locally finite graph GG is given by γG​(R)≔supv∈V⁡(G)|BG​(v,R)|\gamma_{G}(R)\coloneqq\sup_{v\in V(G)}|B_{G}(v,R)|, where BG​(v,R)B_{G}(v,R) is the RR-ball around vv in GG, i.e., the set of all vertices joined to vv by a path of at most RR edges. The quantity

𝖾𝗀𝗋⁡(G)≔limR→∞γG​(R)R=infR⩾1γG​(R)R\mathsf{egr}(G)\,\coloneqq\,\lim_{R\to\infty}\sqrt[R]{\gamma_{G}(R)}\,=\,\inf_{R\geqslant 1}\sqrt[R]{\gamma_{G}(R)}

is called the exponential growth rate of GG. (The limit exists and is equal to the infimum by Fekete’s lemma [42, Lem. A.4.2].) We say that GG is of subexponential growth if 𝖾𝗀𝗋⁡(G)=1\mathsf{egr}(G)=1.

The theorem of Csóka et al. and all the results of this paper apply to Borel CSPs, i.e., CSPs of the form Π=(V,Λ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆,ℬ)\Pi=(V,\Lambda,\mathfrak{C},\mathsf{dom},\mathcal{B}) in which VV, Λ\Lambda, and ℭ\mathfrak{C} are standard Borel spaces and the assignments 𝖽𝗈𝗆\mathsf{dom} and ℬ\mathcal{B} are Borel in a certain natural sense; see §3.1 for the formal definition. Csóka et al. showed that a Borel CSP Π\Pi that fulfills the assumptions of the LLL has a Borel solution, provided that its dependency graph is of subexponential growth and, furthermore, the label set Λ\Lambda and the order of Π\Pi, defined below, are finite.

Definition 1.10 (Order and maximum variable degree).

Let Π=(V,Λ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆,ℬ)\Pi=(V,\Lambda,\mathfrak{C},\mathsf{dom},\mathcal{B}) be a CSP. For v∈Vv\in V, let 𝖽𝗈𝗆−1​(v)≔{𝔠∈ℭ:v∈𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)}\mathsf{dom}^{-1}(v)\coloneqq\{\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}\,:\,v\in\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\}. The order and the maximum variable degree of Π\Pi are

𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡(Π)≔sup𝔠∈ℭ|𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)|and𝗏𝖽𝖾𝗀⁡(Π)≔supv∈V|𝖽𝗈𝗆−1​(v)|.\mathsf{ord}(\Pi)\,\coloneqq\,\sup_{\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}}|\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})|\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathsf{vdeg}(\Pi)\,\coloneqq\,\sup_{v\in V}|\mathsf{dom}^{-1}(v)|.
Theorem 1.11 (Csóka–Grabowski–Máthé–Pikhurko–Tyros [17]).

Let Π=(V,Λ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆,ℬ)\Pi=(V,\Lambda,\mathfrak{C},\mathsf{dom},\mathcal{B}) be a Borel CSP and let ℙ\mathbb{P} be a Borel probability measure on Λ\Lambda. If there are p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1), d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}} such that:

  1. (i)

    ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔠)]⩽p\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})]\leqslant p for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, the maximum degree of DΠD_{\Pi} is at most dd, and 𝖾​p​(d+1)<1\mathsf{e}\,p\,(d+1)<1,

  2. (ii)

    DΠD_{\Pi} is of subexponential growth, and

  3. (iii)

    Λ\Lambda is a finite set and 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡(Π)<∞\mathsf{ord}(\Pi)<\infty,

then Π\Pi has a Borel solution f:V→Λf\colon V\to\Lambda.

In Theorem 1.11, (i) is just the standard LLL assumption (as in Theorem 1.5). Example 1.3 shows that some extra conditions are necessary to guarantee the existence of a Borel solution, and the subexponential growth of DΠD_{\Pi} is a natural requirement to add. Indeed, Theorem 1.11 belongs to a growing body of research showing that various combinatorial problems can be solved in a Borel way on graphs of subexponential growth [16, 44, 3]. For example, Thornton proved that if d⩾3d\geqslant 3, then every dd-regular Borel graph of subexponential growth has a Borel sinkless orientation [44, Thm. 1.5]. For d⩾4d\geqslant 4, this fact is a consequence of Theorem 1.11. Other applications of Theorem 1.11 can be found in [5, 9].

On the other hand, condition (iii) in Theorem 1.11 may seem somewhat puzzling. While it is usually satisfied in combinatorial applications, it is unclear whether its presence is necessary, given that the classical LLL (i.e., Theorem 1.5) is valid even if (Λ,ℙ)(\Lambda,\mathbb{P}) is a continuous probability space. As we explain below, the proof of Theorem 1.11 in [17] uses the finiteness of both Λ\Lambda and 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡(Π)\mathsf{ord}(\Pi) in an essential and apparently unavoidable way. Nevertheless, in this paper we present an alternative proof strategy that completely eliminates assumption (iii):

Theorem 1.11 is a corollary of the following more general statement established in [17], which explicitly invokes the finite values of |Λ||\Lambda| and 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡(Π)\mathsf{ord}(\Pi):

Theorem 1.13 ([17, Thm. 4.5]).

Let Π=(V,Λ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆,ℬ)\Pi=(V,\Lambda,\mathfrak{C},\mathsf{dom},\mathcal{B}) be a Borel CSP such that Λ\Lambda is a nonempty finite set, and let ℙ\mathbb{P} be the uniform probability distribution on Λ\Lambda. Suppose there exist parameters p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1), dd, Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}}, and ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that:

  1. (i)

    ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔠)]⩽p\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})]\leqslant p for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} and the maximum degree of DΠD_{\Pi} is at most dd,

  2. (ii)

    both 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡(Π)\mathsf{ord}(\Pi) and 𝗏𝖽𝖾𝗀⁡(Π)\mathsf{vdeg}(\Pi) are at most Δ\Delta,

  3. (iii)

    𝖾𝗀𝗋⁡(DΠ)<(1+ε)2/3\mathsf{egr}(D_{\Pi})<(1+\varepsilon)^{2/3}, and

  4. (iv)

    𝖾​p​(d+1)​|Λ|ε​Δ<1\mathsf{e}\,p\,(d+1)\,|\Lambda|^{\varepsilon\Delta}<1.

Then Π\Pi has a Borel solution f:V→Λf\colon V\to\Lambda.

Remarks 1.14.
  1. (i)

    Since our notation is somewhat different from that in [17], let us briefly comment on how Theorem 1.13 follows from [17, Thm. 4.5]. Let GG be the bipartite graph with a bipartition (V,ℭ)(V,\mathfrak{C}) such that v∈Vv\in V is adjacent to 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} if and only if v∈𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)v\in\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c}) (this is the construction in [17, Rmk. 1.3]). Condition (ii) of Theorem 1.13 then says that the maximum degree of GG is at most Δ\Delta. It is not hard to see that if 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡(Π)<∞\mathsf{ord}(\Pi)<\infty, then 𝖾𝗀𝗋⁡(DΠ)=𝖾𝗀𝗋​(G)2\mathsf{egr}(D_{\Pi})=\mathsf{egr}(G)^{2}, so (iii) is equivalent to 𝖾𝗀𝗋⁡(G)<(1+ε)1/3\mathsf{egr}(G)<(1+\varepsilon)^{1/3}. This implies that for large enough R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}}, γG​(3​R)<(1+ε)R\gamma_{G}(3R)<(1+\varepsilon)^{R}. In the notation of [17], this means that G∈SubExp⁡(R,ε,Δ)G\in\mathrm{SubExp}(R,\varepsilon,\Delta), and hence [17, Thm. 4.5] may be applied to obtain a Borel solution to Π\Pi.

  2. (ii)

    Let us also sketch how Theorem 1.13 yields Theorem 1.11. Suppose we are in the setting of Theorem 1.11. To begin with, we may replace Π\Pi by an equivalent problem (possibly with a larger set of labels) to arrange that ℙ\mathbb{P} is the uniform probability measure on Λ\Lambda [5, Rmk. 2.4]. Next we note that Δ≔max⁡{𝗏𝖽𝖾𝗀⁡(Π),𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡(Π)}\Delta\coloneqq\max\big\{\mathsf{vdeg}(\Pi),\mathsf{ord}(\Pi)\big\} must be finite, because 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡(Π)<∞\mathsf{ord}(\Pi)<\infty by assumption and 𝗏𝖽𝖾𝗀⁡(Π)⩽d+1\mathsf{vdeg}(\Pi)\leqslant d+1. Hence, we can choose ε>0\varepsilon>0 so small that 𝖾​p​(d+1)<|Λ|−ε​Δ\mathsf{e}\,p\,(d+1)<|\Lambda|^{-\varepsilon\Delta}. Since DΠD_{\Pi} is of subexponential growth, 𝖾𝗀𝗋⁡(DΠ)=1<(1+ε)2/3\mathsf{egr}(D_{\Pi})=1<(1+\varepsilon)^{2/3}, so Π\Pi has a Borel solution by Theorem 1.13.

Note that Theorem 1.13 holds even if the dependency graph DΠD_{\Pi} is of exponential growth, as long as its exponential growth rate is sufficiently small. Unfortunately, how small the growth rate has to be significantly depends on |Λ||\Lambda| and Δ\Delta; that is why both Λ\Lambda and 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡(Π)\mathsf{ord}(\Pi) must be finite for this result to apply. In particular, notice that Theorem 1.13 can only be used when 𝖾𝗀𝗋⁡(DΠ)<22/3≈1.59\mathsf{egr}(D_{\Pi})<2^{2/3}\approx 1.59. Indeed, in the setting of Theorem 1.13, every constraint 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} must satisfy either ℬ⁡(𝔠)=∅\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})=\varnothing or

ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔠)]⩾1|Λ||𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)|⩾1|Λ|𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡(Π)⩾1|Λ|Δ.\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})]\,\geqslant\,\frac{1}{|\Lambda|^{|\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})|}}\,\geqslant\,\frac{1}{|\Lambda|^{\mathsf{ord}(\Pi)}}\,\geqslant\,\frac{1}{|\Lambda|^{\Delta}}.

Therefore, except for the trivial case p=0p=0, we have p⩾|Λ|−Δp\geqslant|\Lambda|^{-\Delta}. Hence, the bound 𝖾​p​(d+1)​|Λ|ε​Δ<1\mathsf{e}\,p\,(d+1)\,|\Lambda|^{\varepsilon\Delta}<1 can only be satisfied if ε<1\varepsilon<1, and thus Theorem 1.13 requires 𝖾𝗀𝗋⁡(DΠ)<22/3\mathsf{egr}(D_{\Pi})<2^{2/3}.

In our main result we remedy the above shortcomings of Theorem 1.13; that is, we generalize it to arbitrary Λ\Lambda, remove the bound on 𝗈𝗋𝖽⁡(Π)\mathsf{ord}(\Pi), and make it applicable to dependency graphs whose exponential growth rate may be arbitrarily large (although it must still be bounded in terms of the relationship between pp and dd):

Theorem 1.12 is an immediate corollary to Theorem 1.15: if 𝖾𝗀𝗋⁡(DΠ)=1\mathsf{egr}(D_{\Pi})=1 and 𝖾​p​(d+1)<1\mathsf{e}\,p\,(d+1)<1, we can find ε>0\varepsilon>0 such that p​(𝖾⁡(d+1))1+ε<1p\,(\mathsf{e}\,(d+1))^{1+\varepsilon}<1 and apply Theorem 1.15 with s=1+εs=1+\varepsilon. Furthermore, it is a standard observation (see, e.g., [2, 8, 15, 19, 20, 4]) that for a majority of applications, instead of the usual LLL condition 𝖾​p​(d+1)<1\mathsf{e}\,p\,(d+1)<1, it is enough to have a version of the LLL that holds under a polynomial criterion, i.e., with a bound of the form p​f​(d)<1p\,f(d)<1 for some polynomial ff. When ss, the bound on the exponential growth rate of DΠD_{\Pi}, is treated as a constant parameter, Theorem 1.15 becomes of this type.

Example 1.16 (Borel sinkless orientation—a positive result).

Consider again the sinkless orientation problem Π∙⁣→​(G)\Pi_{\bullet\to}(G) for a dd-regular Borel graph GG from Examples 1.3 and 1.8. It is easy to see that if every component of GG has a cycle, then GG has a Borel sinkless orientation. Furthermore, when GG is of subexponential growth, Thornton showed that GG has a Borel orientation in which every vertex has outdegree at least d/2−1d/2-1 [44, Thm. 1.5]. Theorem 1.15 yields an extension of this result to graphs whose exponential growth rate is near-linear in dd: For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, GG has a Borel orientation where every vertex has outdegree at least (1−ε)​d/2(1-\varepsilon)d/2, provided that 𝖾𝗀𝗋⁡(G)⩽O⁡(ε2​d/log⁡d)\mathsf{egr}(G)\leqslant O(\varepsilon^{2}d/\log d).

In addition to establishing a more general result, our proof of Theorem 1.15 is also somewhat simpler than the proof of Theorem 1.13 given in [17], although the two arguments have several common ingredients. The starting point of both approaches is the so-called Moser–Tardos Algorithm: a randomized procedure for solving CSPs developed and analyzed by Moser and Tardos in their landmark paper [37]. We give an overview of the Moser–Tardos Algorithm in §2.1. The difficulty in the Borel setting, roughly, is that the Moser–Tardos Algorithm needs a large set of mutually independent random inputs, which cannot be generated in a Borel way. The authors of [17] deal with this challenge via randomness conservation: namely, they reuse the same random input multiple times. With a careful analysis of the Moser–Tardos Algorithm, they are able to show that it still succeeds when randomness is conserved in this way. This step in the proof involves combinatorial counting arguments that are ultimately responsible for the dependence on |Λ||\Lambda| and Δ\Delta in Theorem 1.13. Our strategy is to use probability boosting instead: thanks to the bound on the exponential growth rate of DΠD_{\Pi}, we are able to reduce the given CSP Π\Pi to a different CSP Π′\Pi^{\prime} whose corresponding value of pp is much smaller. This reduction is explained in §2.2, and the desired properties of Π′\Pi^{\prime} are established in §§2.3, 2.4, and 2.5. We then find a Borel solution to Π′\Pi^{\prime}—and hence to Π\Pi—using the following lemma:

Lemma 1.17.

Let Π=(V,Λ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆,ℬ)\Pi=(V,\Lambda,\mathfrak{C},\mathsf{dom},\mathcal{B}) be a Borel CSP and let ℙ\mathbb{P} be a Borel probability measure on Λ\Lambda. Suppose there exist parameters p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1) and d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}} such that:

  • —

    ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔠)]⩽p\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})]\leqslant p for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, the maximum degree of DΠD_{\Pi} is at most dd, and

    p​(d+1)d+1< 1.p\,(d+1)^{d+1}\,<\,1.

Then Π\Pi has a Borel solution f:V→Λf\colon V\to\Lambda.

Lemma 1.17 is proved via the method of conditional probabilities, a standard derandomization technique in computer science [1, 38]. This method has already been applied to obtain “constructive” versions of the LLL in various contexts [2, 19, 4, 10]. Indeed, the proof of Lemma 1.17 is almost exactly the same as that of [10, Thm. 1.6] and [4, Thm. 3.3]. The only difference is that the results in [10, 4] are stated for finite Λ\Lambda; however, their proofs can be adapted for the general case with minimal modifications. For completeness, we present a direct proof of Lemma 1.17 in §3.2. We then finish the proof of Theorem 1.15 in §3.3.

2.  The Moser–Tardos Algorithm and its local analysis

In this section we present the combinatorial heart of our argument. Throughout §2, we fix a CSP Π=(V,Λ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆,ℬ)\Pi=(V,\Lambda,\mathfrak{C},\mathsf{dom},\mathcal{B}) and a probability measure ℙ\mathbb{P} on Λ\Lambda making (Λ,ℙ)(\Lambda,\mathbb{P}) a standard probability space. We also let D≔DΠD\coloneqq D_{\Pi} be the dependency graph of Π\Pi and assume that DD is locally finite. For each 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, we write N⁡[𝔠]≔BD​(𝔠,1)N[\mathfrak{c}]\coloneqq B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},1) and N⁡(𝔠)≔N⁡[𝔠]∖{𝔠}N(\mathfrak{c})\coloneqq N[\mathfrak{c}]\setminus\{\mathfrak{c}\} for the closed, resp. open neighborhood of 𝔠\mathfrak{c} in the graph DD. Note that since DD is locally finite by assumption, N⁡[𝔠]N[\mathfrak{c}] and N⁡(𝔠)N(\mathfrak{c}) are finite sets.

2.1.  The Moser–Tardos Algorithm

As mentioned in the introduction, an important tool in the study of “constructive” aspects of the LLL is the Moser–Tardos Algorithm, or 𝖬𝖳𝖠\mathsf{MTA} for short (see Algorithm 1). It was introduced by Moser and Tardos in [37] in order to prove an algorithmic version of the LLL. 𝖬𝖳𝖠\mathsf{MTA} takes as input a CSP Π\Pi and a map τ:V→Λℕ\tau\colon V\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}}, called a table (we picture it as a matrix with rows indexed by ℕ{\mathbb{N}}, columns indexed by VV, and entries from Λ\Lambda). For convenience, given v∈Vv\in V and n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, we write τ⁡(v,n)\tau(v,n) for the nn-th entry of the sequence τ⁡(v)∈Λℕ\tau(v)\in\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}}. The algorithm attempts to solve Π\Pi by building a sequence of labelings f0f_{0}, f1f_{1}, … :V→Λ\colon V\to\Lambda as follows. We start by setting f0​(v)≔τ⁡(v,0)f_{0}(v)\coloneqq\tau(v,0) for all v∈Vv\in V. At the nn-th iteration, we let ℭn⊆ℭ\mathfrak{C}_{n}\subseteq\mathfrak{C} be the set of all constraints violated by fnf_{n}. We then pick some DD-independent22 2 Recall that a set of vertices in a graph is independent if no two of its members are adjacent. subset ℑn⊆ℭn\mathfrak{I}_{n}\subseteq\mathfrak{C}_{n} and, for each constraint 𝔠∈ℑn\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{I}_{n} and every variable v∈𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)v\in\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c}), update fn​(v)f_{n}(v) to be the next value in the sequence τ⁡(v)\tau(v) (we use a function ℓn:V→ℕ\ell_{n}\colon V\to{\mathbb{N}} to keep track of the current position in the sequence). This produces the labeling fn+1f_{n+1}. Taking a natural limit yields a (possibly partial) labeling ff. The details are presented in Algorithm 1.

Note that Algorithm 1 does not specify how the DD-independent subsets ℑn⊆ℭn\mathfrak{I}_{n}\subseteq\mathfrak{C}_{n} are to be chosen. Hence, the input of 𝖬𝖳𝖠\mathsf{MTA} does not determine the execution process of the algorithm uniquely. We call a sequence ℑ=(ℑn)n∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}=(\mathfrak{I}_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} of DD-independent subsets of ℭ\mathfrak{C} an 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence, and say that an 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence is consistent with (Π,τ)(\Pi,\tau) if it can be produced by 𝖬𝖳𝖠\mathsf{MTA} with input (Π,τ)(\Pi,\tau). It is also possible to give a direct combinatorial description of 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequences consistent with (Π,τ)(\Pi,\tau). To this end, given an 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence ℑ=(ℑn)n∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}=(\mathfrak{I}_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} and 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, we write

Ln​(ℑ,𝔠)≔{i<n:𝔠∈ℑi}.L_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\mathfrak{c})\,\coloneqq\,\{i<n\,:\,\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{I}_{i}\}.
Lemma 2.1.

Let τ\tau be a table and let ℑ\mathfrak{I} be an 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence. For each n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and v∈Vv\in V, let

(2.2) ℓn​(ℑ,v)≔∑𝔠∈𝖽𝗈𝗆−1​(v)|Ln​(ℑ,𝔠)|andfn​(ℑ,v)≔τ⁡(v,ℓn​(v)).\ell_{n}(\mathfrak{I},v)\,\coloneqq\,\sum_{\mathfrak{c}\,\in\,\mathsf{dom}^{-1}(v)}|L_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\mathfrak{c})|\qquad\text{and}\qquad f_{n}(\mathfrak{I},v)\,\coloneqq\,\tau(v,\ell_{n}(v)).

Then ℑ\mathfrak{I} is consistent with (Π,τ)(\Pi,\tau) if and only if for all n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, fn​(ℑ,⋅)f_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\cdot) violates every constraint in ℑn\mathfrak{I}_{n}.

Proof.

If we run 𝖬𝖳𝖠\mathsf{MTA} on input (Π,τ)(\Pi,\tau) with ℑ\mathfrak{I} as the 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence, then the resulting functions ℓn:V→ℕ\ell_{n}\colon V\to{\mathbb{N}} and fn:V→Λf_{n}\colon V\to\Lambda will be precisely given by (2.2). Therefore, choosing ℑn\mathfrak{I}_{n} on step nn of the algorithm is allowed if and only if ℑn⊆ℭn\mathfrak{I}_{n}\subseteq\mathfrak{C}_{n}, i.e., if fnf_{n} violates every constraint in ℑn\mathfrak{I}_{n}. ∎

The Maximal Moser–Tardos Algorithm, or 𝖬𝖬𝖳𝖠\mathsf{MMTA} for short, is a variant of 𝖬𝖳𝖠\mathsf{MTA} with the additional requirement that each set ℑn\mathfrak{I}_{n} be an (inclusion-)maximal DD-independent subset of ℭn\mathfrak{C}_{n} (this is [37, Alg. 1.2]). We write 𝖬𝖳𝖠⁡(Π,τ)\mathsf{MTA}(\Pi,\tau) (resp. 𝖬𝖬𝖳𝖠⁡(Π,τ)\mathsf{MMTA}(\Pi,\tau)) for the set of all partial labelings ff that can be generated by 𝖬𝖳𝖠\mathsf{MTA} (resp. 𝖬𝖬𝖳𝖠\mathsf{MMTA}) on input (Π,τ)(\Pi,\tau). By definition, 𝖬𝖬𝖳𝖠⁡(Π,τ)⊆𝖬𝖳𝖠⁡(Π,τ)\mathsf{MMTA}(\Pi,\tau)\subseteq\mathsf{MTA}(\Pi,\tau).

Lemma 2.3.

Suppose ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔠)]<1\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})]<1 for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} and let τ\tau be a table. If a labeling f∈𝖬𝖬𝖳𝖠⁡(Π,τ)f\in\mathsf{MMTA}(\Pi,\tau) is defined on all of VV, then ff is a solution to Π\Pi.

Proof.

Note that if the domain of a constraint 𝔠\mathfrak{c} is empty, then there are two options for ℬ⁡(𝔠)\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c}), namely ∅\varnothing and {∅}\{\varnothing\}, and we have ℙ⁡[∅]=0\mathbb{P}[\varnothing]=0 and ℙ⁡[{∅}]=1\mathbb{P}[\{\varnothing\}]=1. Since ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔠)]<1\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})]<1 by assumption, we conclude that ℬ⁡(𝔠)=∅\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})=\varnothing. In other words, such a constraint 𝔠\mathfrak{c} is satisfied by every labeling.

Now suppose f∈𝖬𝖬𝖳𝖠⁡(Π,τ)f\in\mathsf{MMTA}(\Pi,\tau) is defined everywhere and violates some constraint 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}. It follows that 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)≠∅\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\neq\varnothing. Let ℓn\ell_{n} and ℓ\ell be as in Algorithm 1, and let n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} be such that ℓ​(v)=ℓn​(v)\ell(v)=\ell_{n}(v) for all v∈𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)v\in\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c}), which exists because ℓ\ell is finite everywhere. Then ff agrees with fnf_{n} on 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c}), so fnf_{n} also violates 𝔠\mathfrak{c}. This implies that 𝔠∈ℭn\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}_{n}, and, by the maximality of ℑn\mathfrak{I}_{n} and since 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)≠∅\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\neq\varnothing, there must be some 𝔠′∈ℑn\mathfrak{c}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{I}_{n} with 𝔠′∈N⁡[𝔠]\mathfrak{c}^{\prime}\in N[\mathfrak{c}]. But then for any v∈𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)∩𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠′)v\in\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\cap\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c}^{\prime}), we have ℓn+1​(v)=ℓn​(v)+1\ell_{n+1}(v)=\ell_{n}(v)+1, contradicting the choice of nn. ∎

2.2.  Good and locally good tables

It follows from Lemma 2.3 that to solve Π\Pi, it is enough to find a table τ\tau such that some labeling f∈𝖬𝖬𝖳𝖠⁡(Π,τ)f\in\mathsf{MMTA}(\Pi,\tau) is defined everywhere. We shall seek a table with the following stronger property:

Definition 2.4 (Good tables).

A table τ\tau is good if every f∈𝖬𝖳𝖠⁡(Π,τ)f\in\mathsf{MTA}(\Pi,\tau) is defined on all of VV.

The following is the main result of [37]:

Theorem 2.5 (Moser–Tardos [37, Thm. 1.2]).

Let pp and dd be as in Theorem 1.5 (i.e., the LLL). Sample a random table τ:V→Λℕ\tau\colon V\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}} from the product space (ΛV×ℕ,ℙV×ℕ)(\Lambda^{V\times{\mathbb{N}}},\mathbb{P}^{V\times{\mathbb{N}}}). Then for each v∈Vv\in V,

ℙ⁡[every f∈𝖬𝖳𝖠⁡(Π,τ) is defined on v]= 1.\mathbb{P}[\text{every $f\in\mathsf{MTA}(\Pi,\tau)$ is defined on $v$}]\,=\,1.

It follows that if VV is finite (or countable), then a random table τ:V→Λℕ\tau\colon V\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}} is almost surely good; in particular, a good table exists. As explained in Remark 1.6(ii), Theorem 1.5 for infinite VV then follows via a compactness argument. Moreover, although the proof of Theorem 2.5 given in [37] assumes VV is finite, it works just as well in the infinite case; see [6, §3] for a detailed presentation of the argument for arbitrary VV. (This was also observed in [41, 34].)

Unfortunately, even though Theorem 2.5 holds for infinite VV, it cannot be applied directly to find a Borel solution to Π\Pi, for two reasons. First, if VV is uncountable, we can no longer conclude that a random table is good with probability 11 (or even with positive probability). Second—and more importantly—a random table would typically not be a Borel function. As mentioned in the introduction, Csóka et al. [17] handled this issue by using the same random values for multiple variables. Namely, they partitioned VV into finitely many “sparse” Borel subsets as V=V1∪…∪VkV=V_{1}\cup\ldots\cup V_{k} and generated a table τ:V→Λℕ\tau\colon V\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}} by independently picking kk random sequences τ1\tau_{1}, …, τk∈Λℕ\tau_{k}\in\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}} and setting τ⁡(v)≔τi\tau(v)\coloneqq\tau_{i} for all v∈Viv\in V_{i}. They then were able to establish a suitable analog of Theorem 2.5 for this construction under the assumptions of Theorem 1.13.

Our approach instead is to treat the problem of finding a good table τ:V→Λℕ\tau\colon V\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}} as a CSP in its own right. The idea is to “localize” the notion of goodness by “zooming in” on rr-balls around individual constraints in the graph DD. To this end, given 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} and r∈ℕr\in{\mathbb{N}}, we define the (𝔠,r)(\mathfrak{c},r)-local CSP Π𝔠,r≔(V,Λ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆,ℬ𝔠,r)\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r}\coloneqq(V,\Lambda,\mathfrak{C},\mathsf{dom},\mathcal{B}_{\mathfrak{c},r}) by letting, for all 𝔞∈ℭ\mathfrak{a}\in\mathfrak{C},

ℬ𝔠,r​(𝔞)≔{ℬ⁡(𝔞)if ​𝔞∈BD​(𝔠,r),Λ𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔞)otherwise.\mathcal{B}_{\mathfrak{c},r}(\mathfrak{a})\,\coloneqq\,\begin{cases}\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a})&\text{if }\mathfrak{a}\in B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r),\\ \Lambda^{\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{a})}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

That is, from the point of view of Π𝔠,r\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r}, the constraints at distance more than rr from 𝔠\mathfrak{c} in DD are always violated. In particular, to check whether an 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence is consistent with (Π𝔠,r,τ)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau), we only need to consider the constraints in BD​(𝔠,r)B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r):

Lemma 2.6.

Let τ\tau be a table and let ℑ\mathfrak{I} be an 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence. For each n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and v∈Vv\in V, define ℓn​(ℑ,v)\ell_{n}(\mathfrak{I},v) and fn​(ℑ,v)f_{n}(\mathfrak{I},v) as in (2.2). Then, for any 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} and r∈ℕr\in{\mathbb{N}}, ℑ\mathfrak{I} is consistent with (Π𝔠,r,τ)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau) if and only if for all n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, fn​(ℑ,⋅)f_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\cdot) violates every constraint in ℑn∩BD​(𝔠,r)\mathfrak{I}_{n}\cap B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r).

Proof.

Follows immediately by applying Lemma 2.1 with Π𝔠,r\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r} in place of Π\Pi. ∎

It is clear that, unless BD​(𝔠,r)=ℭB_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r)=\mathfrak{C}, the CSP Π𝔠,r\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r} has no solutions, because the constraints in ℭ∖BD​(𝔠,r)\mathfrak{C}\setminus B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r) are, by definition, always violated. In particular, the Moser–Tardos Algorithm must fail to generate a solution to Π𝔠,r\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r}. However, we may ask whether the constraints in ℭ∖BD​(𝔠,r)\mathfrak{C}\setminus B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r) are in some sense the “main reason” for this failure. Namely, if ℑ=(ℑn)n∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}=(\mathfrak{I}_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} is an 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence consistent with (Π𝔠,r,τ)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau), must it be that “many” constraints in the sets ℑn\mathfrak{I}_{n} come from outside BD​(𝔠,r)B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r)?

In order to quantify the word “many” in the preceding sentence, we restrict our attention to finite 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequences, i.e., 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequences ℑ=(ℑn)n∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}=(\mathfrak{I}_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} such that ∑n∈ℕ|ℑn|<∞\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}_{n}|<\infty. In other words, ℑ\mathfrak{I} is finite if each ℑn\mathfrak{I}_{n} is a finite set and ℑn=∅\mathfrak{I}_{n}=\varnothing for all large enough n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}. Now, if ℑ=(ℑn)n∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}=(\mathfrak{I}_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} is a finite 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence consistent with (Π𝔠,r,τ)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau), we can consider the sets

ℑn∩BD​(𝔠,r)andℑn∖BD​(𝔠,r)\mathfrak{I}_{n}\cap B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathfrak{I}_{n}\setminus B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r)

for each n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, and we want the former ones to not be much larger than the latter. Formally, we say a finite 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence ℑ=(ℑn)n∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}=(\mathfrak{I}_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} is (𝔠,r,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},r,N,\varepsilon)-Følner for 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, rr, N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}}, and ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) if

∑n∈ℕ|ℑn∩BD​(𝔠,r)|⩾Nand∑n∈ℕ|ℑn∖BD​(𝔠,r)|<ε​∑n∈ℕ|ℑn|.\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}_{n}\cap B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r)|\,\geqslant\,N\qquad\text{and}\qquad\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}_{n}\setminus B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r)|\,<\,\varepsilon\sum_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}_{n}|.
Definition 2.7 (Locally good tables).

Fix 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, RR, N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}}, and ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1). A table τ:V→Λℕ\tau\colon V\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}} is (𝔠,R,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good if for all 0⩽r<R0\leqslant r<R, there is no (𝔠,r,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},r,N,\varepsilon)-Følner 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence consistent with (Π𝔠,r,τ)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau). A table τ\tau is (R,N,ε)(R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good if it is (𝔠,R,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}.

The following lemma, proved in §2.4, is the only place where we use a bound on 𝖾𝗀𝗋⁡(D)\mathsf{egr}(D):

Lemma 2.8.

Let R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}} and ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) be such that γD​(R)<(1−ε)−R\gamma_{D}(R)<(1-\varepsilon)^{-R}, where γD\gamma_{D} is the growth function of DD. If a table τ:V→Λℕ\tau\colon V\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}} is (R,N,ε)(R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good for some N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}}, then τ\tau is good.

Next we construct a CSP 𝖫𝖦⁡(R,N,ε)\mathsf{LG}(R,N,\varepsilon) with label set Λℕ\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}} such that a table τ:V→Λℕ\tau\colon V\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}} is a solution to 𝖫𝖦⁡(R,N,ε)\mathsf{LG}(R,N,\varepsilon) if and only if τ\tau is (R,N,ε)(R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good. To this end, we define

𝖫𝖦⁡(R,N,ε)≔(V,Λℕ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆R,ℒR,N,ε),\mathsf{LG}(R,N,\varepsilon)\,\coloneqq\,\big(V,\,\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}},\,\mathfrak{C},\,\mathsf{dom}_{R},\,\mathcal{L}_{R,N,\varepsilon}\big),

where for each 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, 𝖽𝗈𝗆R​(𝔠)≔⋃𝔞∈BD​(𝔠,R)𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔞)\mathsf{dom}_{R}(\mathfrak{c})\coloneqq\bigcup_{\mathfrak{a}\in B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},R)}\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{a}) and ℒR,N,ε\mathcal{L}_{R,N,\varepsilon} is given by the following:

Lemma 2.9.

Fix 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, RR, N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}}, and ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1). If tables τ0\tau_{0}, τ1:V→Λℕ\tau_{1}\colon V\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}} agree on 𝖽𝗈𝗆R​(𝔠)\mathsf{dom}_{R}(\mathfrak{c}), then

τ0 is (𝔠,R,N,ε)-locally good⟺τ1 is (𝔠,R,N,ε)-locally good.\text{$\tau_{0}$ is $(\mathfrak{c},R,N,\varepsilon)$-locally good}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\text{$\tau_{1}$ is $(\mathfrak{c},R,N,\varepsilon)$-locally good}.

Therefore, there is a set ℒR,N,ε​(𝔠)⊆(Λℕ)𝖽𝗈𝗆R​(𝔠)\mathcal{L}_{R,N,\varepsilon}(\mathfrak{c})\subseteq(\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}})^{\mathsf{dom}_{R}(\mathfrak{c})} such that for any φ:𝖽𝗈𝗆R​(𝔠)→Λℕ\varphi\colon\mathsf{dom}_{R}(\mathfrak{c})\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}}, the following statements are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    some table extending φ\varphi is not (𝔠,R,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good,

  2. (ii)

    every table extending φ\varphi is not (𝔠,R,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good,

  3. (iii)

    φ∈ℒR,N,ε​(𝔠)\varphi\in\mathcal{L}_{R,N,\varepsilon}(\mathfrak{c}).

Proof.

If τ0\tau_{0} is not (𝔠,R,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good, then for some r<Rr<R, there is a (𝔠,r,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},r,N,\varepsilon)-Følner 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence ℑ\mathfrak{I} consistent with (Π𝔠,r,τ0)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau_{0}). Since τ0\tau_{0} and τ1\tau_{1} agree on 𝖽𝗈𝗆r​(𝔠)\mathsf{dom}_{r}(\mathfrak{c}), Lemma 2.6 shows that ℑ\mathfrak{I} is consistent with (Π𝔠,r,τ1)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau_{1}) as well. Hence, τ1\tau_{1} is also not (𝔠,R,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good, as claimed. ∎

It follows from Lemma 2.9 that a table τ:V→Λℕ\tau\colon V\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}} is a solution to 𝖫𝖦⁡(R,N,ε)\mathsf{LG}(R,N,\varepsilon) if and only if τ\tau is (R,N,ε)(R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good, as intended.

Next we proceed to bound the maximum degree of the dependency graph of 𝖫𝖦⁡(R,N,ε)\mathsf{LG}(R,N,\varepsilon):

Lemma 2.10.

For any RR, N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}} and ε>0\varepsilon>0, the maximum degree of the dependency graph of 𝖫𝖦⁡(R,N,ε)\mathsf{LG}(R,N,\varepsilon) is at most γD​(2​R+1)−1\gamma_{D}(2R+1)-1.

Proof.

Distinct constraints 𝔠\mathfrak{c}, 𝔠′∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}^{\prime}\in\mathfrak{C} are adjacent in the dependency graph of 𝖫𝖦⁡(R,N,ε)\mathsf{LG}(R,N,\varepsilon) if and only if 𝖽𝗈𝗆R​(𝔠)∩𝖽𝗈𝗆R​(𝔠′)≠∅\mathsf{dom}_{R}(\mathfrak{c})\cap\mathsf{dom}_{R}(\mathfrak{c}^{\prime})\neq\varnothing, which means that for some 𝔞∈BD​(𝔠,R)\mathfrak{a}\in B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},R) and 𝔞′∈BD​(𝔠′,R)\mathfrak{a}^{\prime}\in B_{D}(\mathfrak{c}^{\prime},R), we have 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔞)∩𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔞′)≠∅\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{a})\cap\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{a}^{\prime})\neq\varnothing, i.e., 𝔞′∈BD​(𝔞,1)\mathfrak{a}^{\prime}\in B_{D}(\mathfrak{a},1). The latter condition implies that 𝔠′∈BD​(𝔠,2​R+1)∖{𝔠}\mathfrak{c}^{\prime}\in B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},2R+1)\setminus\{\mathfrak{c}\}. Since |BD​(𝔠,2​R+1)|⩽γD​(2​R+1)|B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},2R+1)|\leqslant\gamma_{D}(2R+1), the result follows. ∎

The only consequence of Lemma 2.10 we need is that the maximum degree of the dependency graph of 𝖫𝖦⁡(R,N,ε)\mathsf{LG}(R,N,\varepsilon) can be bounded by a function of RR independent of NN. By contrast, we will show that ℙ​[ℒR,N,ε​(𝔠)]\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{L}_{R,N,\varepsilon}(\mathfrak{c})] is bounded above by a quantity that goes to 00 as N→∞N\to\infty (in fact, it goes to 00 exponentially quickly, but that is not important for our purposes):

Lemma 2.11.

Suppose there exist p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1), d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}}, s>1s>1, and ε\varepsilon, η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1) such that:

  1. (i)

    ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔠)]⩽p\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})]\leqslant p for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, the maximum degree of DD is at most dd, and p​(𝖾⁡(d+1))s<1p\,(\mathsf{e}\,(d+1))^{s}<1,

  2. (ii)

    ε+1s<1\displaystyle\varepsilon+\frac{1}{s}<1 and p1−ε−1s⩽1−η1+η\displaystyle p^{1-\varepsilon-\frac{1}{s}}\leqslant\frac{1-\eta}{1+\eta}.

Then for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} and RR, N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}}, we have ℙ⁡[ℒR,N,ε​(𝔠)]⩽(1+η)−N​F​(d,η,R)\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{L}_{R,N,\varepsilon}(\mathfrak{c})]\leqslant(1+\eta)^{-N}\,F(d,\eta,R), where the quantity F⁡(d,η,R)F(d,\eta,R) is independent of NN.

We prove Lemma 2.11 in §2.5.

Using Lemmas 2.10 and 2.11, for any fixed RR, we are able to pick N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}} so large that 𝖫𝖦⁡(R,N,ε)\mathsf{LG}(R,N,\varepsilon) satisfies the assumptions of Lemma 1.17. As a result, we can find a Borel (R,N,ε)(R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good table τ\tau—which must be good by Lemma 2.8—and use it to finish the proof of Theorem 1.15. The details of this part of the argument, as well as the proof of Lemma 1.17, are presented in §3.

2.3.  Preliminary facts about tables and MT\mathsf{MT}-sequences

The following observation will be useful:

Lemma 2.12.

Fix 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} and r∈ℕr\in{\mathbb{N}}. Let ℑ=(ℑn)n∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}=(\mathfrak{I}_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} be an 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence consistent with (Π𝔠,r,τ)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau) for some table τ\tau. Then, for any R>rR>r, ℑ′≔(ℑn∩BD​(𝔠,R))n∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}^{\prime}\coloneqq(\mathfrak{I}_{n}\cap B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},R))_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} is also consistent with (Π𝔠,r,τ)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau).

Proof.

Recall for all 𝔞∈ℭ\mathfrak{a}\in\mathfrak{C} and n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} the notation

Ln​(ℑ,𝔞)≔{i<n:𝔞∈ℑi}andLn​(ℑ′,𝔞)≔{i<n:𝔞∈ℑi′}.L_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\mathfrak{a})\,\coloneqq\,\{i<n\,:\,\mathfrak{a}\in\mathfrak{I}_{i}\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad L_{n}(\mathfrak{I}^{\prime},\mathfrak{a})\,\coloneqq\,\{i<n\,:\,\mathfrak{a}\in\mathfrak{I}_{i}^{\prime}\}.

For each n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and v∈Vv\in V, let fn​(ℑ,v)f_{n}(\mathfrak{I},v) and fn​(ℑ′,v)f_{n}(\mathfrak{I}^{\prime},v) be defined according to (2.2). By Lemma 2.6, we need to show that for all 𝔞∈ℑn′∩BD​(𝔠,r)=ℑn∩BD​(𝔠,r)\mathfrak{a}\in\mathfrak{I}^{\prime}_{n}\cap B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r)=\mathfrak{I}_{n}\cap B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r), the function fn​(ℑ′,⋅)f_{n}(\mathfrak{I}^{\prime},\cdot) violates 𝔞\mathfrak{a}. To this end, note that if v∈𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔞)v\in\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{a}), then every constraint 𝔟∈𝖽𝗈𝗆−1​(v)\mathfrak{b}\in\mathsf{dom}^{-1}(v) belongs to BD​(𝔠,r+1)⊆BD​(𝔠,R)B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r+1)\subseteq B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},R), and hence Ln​(ℑ′,𝔟)=Ln​(ℑ,𝔟)L_{n}(\mathfrak{I}^{\prime},\mathfrak{b})=L_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\mathfrak{b}). It follows that fn​(ℑ′,v)=fn​(ℑ,v)f_{n}(\mathfrak{I}^{\prime},v)=f_{n}(\mathfrak{I},v). Since ℑ\mathfrak{I} is consistent with (Π𝔠,r,τ)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau), fn​(ℑ,⋅)f_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\cdot) violates 𝔞\mathfrak{a} by Lemma 2.6, which implies that fn​(ℑ′,⋅)f_{n}(\mathfrak{I}^{\prime},\cdot) violates 𝔞\mathfrak{a} as well, as desired. ∎

A consequence of Lemma 2.12 is that the property of being (𝔠,R,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good for a table τ\tau is “localized” in the graph DD, in the sense that it only involves the constraints in BD​(𝔠,R)B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},R). To make this statement precise, we say that an 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence ℑ=(ℑn)n∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}=(\mathfrak{I}_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} is (𝔠,R)(\mathfrak{c},R)-bounded for some 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} and R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}} if ℑn⊆BD​(𝔠,R)\mathfrak{I}_{n}\subseteq B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},R) for all n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}.

Lemma 2.13.

Fix 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, RR, N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}}, and ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1). A table τ\tau is (𝔠,R,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good if and only if for all r<Rr<R, no (𝔠,R)(\mathfrak{c},R)-bounded (𝔠,r,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},r,N,\varepsilon)-Følner 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence ℑ\mathfrak{I} is consistent with (Π𝔠,r,τ)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau).

Proof.

If τ\tau is (𝔠,R,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good, then such an 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence ℑ\mathfrak{I} does not exist by definition. Now suppose τ\tau is not (𝔠,R,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good and let ℑ=(ℑn)n∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}=(\mathfrak{I}_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} be a (𝔠,r,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},r,N,\varepsilon)-Følner 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence consistent with (Π𝔠,r,τ)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau). Then the 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence ℑ′≔(ℑn∩BD​(𝔠,R))n∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}^{\prime}\coloneqq(\mathfrak{I}_{n}\cap B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},R))_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} is also consistent with (Π𝔠,r,τ)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau) by Lemma 2.12, and it is (𝔠,r,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},r,N,\varepsilon)-Følner and (𝔠,R)(\mathfrak{c},R)-bounded, as desired. ∎

2.4.  Locally good implies good: Proof of Lemma 2.8

Let R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}} and ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) be such that γD​(R)<(1−ε)−R\gamma_{D}(R)<(1-\varepsilon)^{-R} and let τ:V→Λℕ\tau\colon V\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}} be an (R,N,ε)(R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good table for some N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}}. Our goal is to show that τ\tau is good.

Assume, toward a contradiction, that there is a labeling f∈𝖬𝖳𝖠⁡(Π,τ)f\in\mathsf{MTA}(\Pi,\tau) whose domain is not all of VV and let ℑ=(ℑn)n∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}=(\mathfrak{I}_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} be the 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence consistent with (Π,τ)(\Pi,\tau) used to generate ff. Recall for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} and n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} the notation Ln​(ℑ,𝔠)≔{i<n:𝔠∈ℑi}L_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\mathfrak{c})\,\coloneqq\,\{i<n\,:\,\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{I}_{i}\}. If ℓn\ell_{n} and ℓ\ell are as in Algorithm 1, then

ℓn​(v)=∑𝔠∈𝖽𝗈𝗆−1​(v)|Ln​(ℑ,𝔠)|.\ell_{n}(v)\,=\,\sum_{\mathfrak{c}\,\in\,\mathsf{dom}^{-1}(v)}|L_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\mathfrak{c})|.

Since ℓ⁡(v)=∞\ell(v)=\infty for some v∈Vv\in V and |𝖽𝗈𝗆−1​(v)|⩽d+1|\mathsf{dom}^{-1}(v)|\leqslant d+1 for all v∈Vv\in V, there must be n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} such that |Ln​(ℑ,𝔠)|>N|L_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\mathfrak{c})|>N. We fix any such n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}} and choose 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} to maximize |Ln​(ℑ,𝔠)||L_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\mathfrak{c})|.

For each integer −1⩽r<R-1\leqslant r<R, we define a finite 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence ℑr=(ℑir)i∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}^{r}=(\mathfrak{I}^{r}_{i})_{i\in{\mathbb{N}}} via

ℑir≔{ℑi∩BD​(𝔠,r+1)if ​i<n,∅if ​i⩾n.\mathfrak{I}^{r}_{i}\,\coloneqq\,\begin{cases}\mathfrak{I}_{i}\cap B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r+1)&\text{if }i<n,\\ \varnothing&\text{if }i\geqslant n.\end{cases}

Consider any 0⩽r<R0\leqslant r<R. Since ℑ\mathfrak{I} is consistent with (Π,τ)(\Pi,\tau) and hence also with (Π𝔠,r,τ)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau), Lemma 2.12 shows that ℑr\mathfrak{I}^{r} is consistent with (Π𝔠,r,τ)(\Pi_{\mathfrak{c},r},\tau). Furthermore, note that

∑i∈ℕ|ℑir∩BD​(𝔠,r)|=∑i∈ℕ|ℑir−1|⩾∑i∈ℕ|ℑi−1|=|Ln​(ℑ,𝔠)|>N.\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}_{i}^{r}\cap B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r)|\,=\,\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}_{i}^{r-1}|\,\geqslant\,\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}^{-1}_{i}|\,=\,|L_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\mathfrak{c})|\,>\,N.

Since τ\tau is (R,N,ε)(R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good, ℑr\mathfrak{I}^{r} cannot be (𝔠,r,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},r,N,\varepsilon)-Følner, and hence

∑i∈ℕ|ℑir∖BD​(𝔠,r)|⩾ε​∑i∈ℕ|ℑir|.\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}_{i}^{r}\setminus B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r)|\,\geqslant\,\varepsilon\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}_{i}^{r}|.

This implies that, for 0⩽r<R0\leqslant r<R,

∑i∈ℕ|ℑir|⩾11−ε​∑i∈ℕ|ℑir∩BD​(𝔠,r)|=11−ε​∑i∈ℕ|ℑir−1|.\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}_{i}^{r}|\,\geqslant\,\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}\,\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}_{i}^{r}\cap B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},r)|\,=\,\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}\,\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}_{i}^{r-1}|.

Applying this inequality iteratively, we obtain

(2.14) ∑i∈ℕ|ℑiR−1|⩾(11−ε)R​∑i∈ℕ|ℑi−1|=(11−ε)R​|Ln​(ℑ,𝔠)|.\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}_{i}^{R-1}|\,\geqslant\,\left(\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}\right)^{R}\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}^{-1}_{i}|\,=\,\left(\frac{1}{1-\varepsilon}\right)^{R}|L_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\mathfrak{c})|.

On the other hand,

(2.15) ∑i∈ℕ|ℑiR−1|=∑𝔞∈BD​(𝔠,R)|Ln​(ℑ,𝔞)|⩽|BD​(𝔠,R)|​|Ln​(ℑ,𝔠)|⩽γD​(R)​|Ln​(ℑ,𝔠)|\sum_{i\in{\mathbb{N}}}|\mathfrak{I}_{i}^{R-1}|\,=\,\sum_{\mathfrak{a}\in B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},R)}|L_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\mathfrak{a})|\,\leqslant\,|B_{D}(\mathfrak{c},R)|\,|L_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\mathfrak{c})|\,\leqslant\,\gamma_{D}(R)\,|L_{n}(\mathfrak{I},\mathfrak{c})|

by the choice of 𝔠\mathfrak{c}. Combining (2.14) and (2.15), we get γD​(R)⩾(1−ε)−R\gamma_{D}(R)\geqslant(1-\varepsilon)^{-R}, which is a contradiction. The proof of Lemma 2.8 is complete.

2.5.  Witness digraphs and the proof of Lemma 2.11

Our proof of Lemma 2.11 relies, in a black box manner, on certain basic results originating in the work of Moser and Tardos [37]. The central idea of Moser–Tardos theory is to analyze 𝖬𝖳𝖠\mathsf{MTA} by means of certain witness structures that keep track of 𝖬𝖳𝖠\mathsf{MTA}’s execution process. One can find several types of such structures in the literature, e.g., the witness trees from the original paper [37], stable set sequences [33], neat piles [6], and witness digraphs [23]. The latter will be especially convenient for our purposes, although it must be stressed that all these different structures are essentially equivalent and can be straightforwardly converted into each other.

The definition of a witness digraph appeared implicitly in the paper [33] by Kolipaka and Szegedy and was formalized in [23] by Haeupler and Harris. See [25, 24, 26, 28] for a selection of other works that rely on this notion.

In the sequel, a digraph means a simple directed graph. A decorated digraph is a digraph Γ\Gamma equipped with a mapping δ:V⁡(Γ)→ℭ\updelta\colon V(\Gamma)\to\mathfrak{C}, called a decoration. We shall always use the symbol δ\updelta to denote the decoration on a decorated digraph. Isomorphisms between decorated digraphs are required to preserve the decoration.

To each finite 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence we associate a decorated digraph called its full witness digraph:

Definition 2.16 (Full witness digraph).

Let ℑ=(ℑn)n∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}=(\mathfrak{I}_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} be a finite 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence. The full witness digraph of ℑ\mathfrak{I} is the finite decorated digraph Γ⁡(ℑ)\Gamma(\mathfrak{I}) defined as follows. The vertex set of Γ⁡(ℑ)\Gamma(\mathfrak{I}) is

V(Γ(ℑ))≔{(n,𝔠):n∈ℕ,𝔠∈ℑn}.V(\Gamma({\mathfrak{I}}))\,\coloneqq\,\big\{(n,\mathfrak{c})\,:\,n\in{\mathbb{N}},\,\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{I}_{n}\big\}.

There is a directed edge from (n,𝔠)(n,\mathfrak{c}) to (n′,𝔠′)(n^{\prime},\mathfrak{c}^{\prime}) in Γ⁡(ℑ)\Gamma({\mathfrak{I}}) if and only if n<n′n<n^{\prime} and 𝔠∈N⁡[𝔠′]\mathfrak{c}\in N[\mathfrak{c}^{\prime}]. The decoration δ\updelta of Γ⁡(ℑ)\Gamma({\mathfrak{I}}) is given by δ⁡(n,𝔠)≔𝔠\updelta(n,\mathfrak{c})\coloneqq\mathfrak{c} for all vertices (n,𝔠)(n,\mathfrak{c}).

Lemma 2.17.

Let ℑ=(ℑn)n∈ℕ\mathfrak{I}=(\mathfrak{I}_{n})_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}} be a finite 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence and let Γ≔Γ⁡(ℑ)\Gamma\coloneqq\Gamma(\mathfrak{I}). Then:

  1. (i)

    Γ\Gamma has no directed cycles,

  2. (ii)

    for all xx, y∈V⁡(Γ)y\in V(\Gamma), (x,y)∈E⁡(Γ)(x,y)\in E(\Gamma) or (y,x)∈E⁡(Γ)(y,x)\in E(\Gamma) if and only if x≠yx\neq y and δ⁡(x)∈N⁡[δ⁡(y)]\updelta(x)\in N[\updelta(y)].

Proof.

If (x,y)∈E⁡(Γ)(x,y)\in E(\Gamma), then the first coordinate of xx is strictly less than the first coordinate of yy, so no directed cycle is possible. Item (ii) is immediate from the way the edge set of Γ\Gamma is defined. ∎

We call a finite decorated digraph Γ\Gamma satisfying conditions (i) and (ii) of Lemma 2.17 a witness digraph. Thus, Lemma 2.17 says that the full witness digraph of a finite 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence is a witness digraph. Now we relate witness digraphs and tables:

Definition 2.18 (Compatible witness digraphs).

A witness digraph Γ\Gamma is compatible with (Π,τ)(\Pi,\tau), where τ\tau is a table, if there exists an 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequence ℑ\mathfrak{I} consistent with (Π,τ)(\Pi,\tau) such that Γ≅Γ⁡(ℑ)\Gamma\cong\Gamma(\mathfrak{I}).

The next result, which we call the First Fundamental Theorem of Moser–Tardos theory, computes the probability that a given witness digraph is compatible with (Π,τ)(\Pi,\tau) for random τ\tau:

Theorem 2.19 (First Fundamental Theorem [23, Prop. 2.5]).

Sample a random table τ:V→Λℕ\tau\colon V\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}} from the space (ΛV×ℕ,ℙV×ℕ)(\Lambda^{V\times{\mathbb{N}}},\mathbb{P}^{V\times{\mathbb{N}}}). Then, for every witness digraph Γ\Gamma, we have

ℙ⁡[Γ​ is compatible with ​(Π,τ)]=∏x∈V⁡(Γ)ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(δ⁡(x))].\mathbb{P}[\Gamma\text{ is compatible with }(\Pi,\tau)]\,=\,\prod_{x\in V(\Gamma)}\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\updelta(x))].

Given a constraint 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, we let 𝖲𝗂𝗇𝗄⁡(𝔠)\mathsf{Sink}(\mathfrak{c}) be the class of all witness digraphs Γ\Gamma such that Γ\Gamma has a single sink σ∈V⁡(Γ)\sigma\in V(\Gamma) and δ⁡(σ)=𝔠\updelta(\sigma)=\mathfrak{c}. We also let 𝖲𝗂𝗇𝗄∗​(𝔠)\mathsf{Sink}^{\ast}(\mathfrak{c}) be a set containing exactly one representative from each isomorphism class of witness digraphs in 𝖲𝗂𝗇𝗄⁡(𝔠)\mathsf{Sink}(\mathfrak{c}). The Second Fundamental Theorem of Moser–Tardos theory is a purely algebraic statement that allows one to bound the quantities appearing in Theorem 2.19 for Γ∈𝖲𝗂𝗇𝗄∗​(𝔠)\Gamma\in\mathsf{Sink}^{*}(\mathfrak{c}):

Theorem 2.20 (Second Fundamental Theorem [23, Prop. 2.10]).

Suppose α\alpha, β:ℭ→[0,1)\beta\colon\mathfrak{C}\to[0,1) are functions such that for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C},

α⁡(𝔠)⩽β⁡(𝔠)​∏𝔠′∈N⁡(𝔠)(1−β⁡(𝔠′)).\alpha(\mathfrak{c})\,\leqslant\,\beta(\mathfrak{c})\prod_{\mathfrak{c}^{\prime}\in N(\mathfrak{c})}(1-\beta(\mathfrak{c}^{\prime})).

Then for each 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C},

∑Γ∈𝖲𝗂𝗇𝗄∗​(𝔠)∏x∈V⁡(Γ)α⁡(δ⁡(x))⩽β⁡(𝔠)1−β⁡(𝔠).\sum_{\Gamma\in\mathsf{Sink}^{\ast}(\mathfrak{c})}\,\prod_{x\in V(\Gamma)}\alpha(\updelta(x))\,\leqslant\,\frac{\beta(\mathfrak{c})}{1-\beta(\mathfrak{c})}.

Theorems 2.19 and 2.20 are essentially present in the seminal paper [37], cf. [37, Lem. 2.1 and 3.1]; the formulations using witness digraphs were given in [23].

We now have all the tools needed to prove Lemma 2.11.

3.  Solving Borel CSPs

3.1.  Preliminaries

In §3 we assume some basic familiarity with descriptive set theory. As mentioned in the introduction, the reader is directed to [32, 45] for the necessary background. In particular, we shall make significant use of the material in [32, Chap. 17 and 18].

In this subsection we give the formal definition of a Borel CSP. To begin with, for a standard Borel space XX and n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, we let [X]n[X]^{n} (resp. [X]<∞[X]^{<\infty}) be the set of all nn-element (resp. finite) subsets of XX. Both [X]n[X]^{n} and [X]<∞[X]^{<\infty} are naturally endowed with standard Borel structures. Namely, we let (X)n⊆Xn(X)^{n}\subseteq X^{n} be the Borel set of all ordered nn-tuples of pairwise distinct points and define an equivalence relation ∼n\sim_{n} on (X)n(X)^{n} by

(x0,…,xn−1)∼n(y0,…,yn−1)⟺{x0,…,xn−1}={y0,…,yn−1}.(x_{0},\ldots,x_{n-1})\,\sim_{n}\,(y_{0},\ldots,y_{n-1})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\{x_{0},\ldots,x_{n-1}\}\,=\,\{y_{0},\ldots,y_{n-1}\}.

By [30, Ex. 6.1 and Prop. 6.3], the quotient space (X)n/∼n≅[X]n(X)^{n}/{\sim_{n}}\cong[X]^{n} is standard Borel. Hence, the disjoint union [X]<∞=[X]0∪[X]1∪[X]2∪…[X]^{<\infty}=[X]^{0}\cup[X]^{1}\cup[X]^{2}\cup\ldots is standard Borel as well [45, Prop. 1.4].

Next, given standard Borel spaces XX and YY, we let [X⇢Y]<∞[{X}\dashrightarrow{Y}]^{<\infty} be the set of all partial maps φ:X⇢Y\varphi\colon X\dashrightarrow Y with finite domains. Identifying each such map φ\varphi with its graph, i.e., with the set

{(x,φ⁡(x)):x∈𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(φ)}⊆X×Y,\{(x,\varphi(x))\,:\,x\in\mathsf{dom}(\varphi)\}\,\subseteq\,X\times Y,

makes [X⇢Y]<∞[{X}\dashrightarrow{Y}]^{<\infty} a Borel subset of [X×Y]<∞[X\times Y]^{<\infty} and hence a standard Borel space in its own right.

Now we can formally define Borel CSPs:

Definition 3.1 (Borel CSPs).

A CSP Π=(V,Λ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆,ℬ)\Pi=(V,\Lambda,\mathfrak{C},\mathsf{dom},\mathcal{B}) is Borel if:

  • —

    VV, Λ\Lambda, and ℭ\mathfrak{C} are standard Borel spaces,

  • —

    the function 𝖽𝗈𝗆:ℭ→[V]<∞\mathsf{dom}\colon\mathfrak{C}\to[V]^{<\infty} is Borel,

  • —

    the set {(𝔠,φ)∈ℭ×[V⇢Λ]<∞:φ∈ℬ(𝔠)}\{(\mathfrak{c},\varphi)\in\mathfrak{C}\times[{V}\dashrightarrow{\Lambda}]^{<\infty}\,:\,\varphi\in\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})\} is Borel.

A graph GG is Borel if V⁡(G)V(G) is a standard Borel space and E⁡(G)E(G) is a Borel subset of [V⁡(G)]2[V(G)]^{2}. It is routine to check that if Π\Pi is a Borel CSP, then its dependency graph DΠD_{\Pi} is Borel.

For the remainder of §3, we let Π=(V,Λ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆,ℬ)\Pi=(V,\Lambda,\mathfrak{C},\mathsf{dom},\mathcal{B}) be a Borel CSP and fix a Borel probability measure ℙ\mathbb{P} on Λ\Lambda. As in §2, we write D≔DΠD\coloneqq D_{\Pi} and let N⁡[𝔠]N[\mathfrak{c}] be the closed neighborhood of a constraint 𝔠\mathfrak{c} in DD. Given a set 𝔘⊆ℭ\mathfrak{U}\subseteq\mathfrak{C}, we let 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔘)≔⋃𝔠∈𝔘𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{U})\coloneqq\bigcup_{\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{U}}\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c}) and N⁡[𝔘]≔⋃𝔠∈𝔘N⁡[𝔠]N[\mathfrak{U}]\coloneqq\bigcup_{\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{U}}N[\mathfrak{c}]. Note that if DD is locally finite and 𝔘⊆ℭ\mathfrak{U}\subseteq\mathfrak{C} is Borel, then the sets 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔘)\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{U}) and N⁡[𝔘]N[\mathfrak{U}] are also Borel by the Luzin–Novikov theorem [32, Thm. 18.10].

3.2.  Proof of Lemma 1.17

We start with a simple observation, which is a consequence of a standard “large section” uniformization result in descriptive set theory [32, §18.B]:

Lemma 3.2.

If DD has no edges and ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔠)]<1\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})]<1 for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, then Π\Pi has a Borel solution.

Proof.

Since ℙ⁡[Λ𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)∖ℬ⁡(𝔠)]>0\mathbb{P}[\Lambda^{\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})}\setminus\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})]>0 for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, by [32, Corl. 18.7], there is a Borel function

F:ℭ→[V⇢Λ]<∞F\colon\mathfrak{C}\to[{V}\dashrightarrow{\Lambda}]^{<\infty}

such that F⁡(𝔠)∈Λ𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)∖ℬ⁡(𝔠)F(\mathfrak{c})\in\Lambda^{\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})}\setminus\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c}) for every constraint 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}. Since DD has no edges (i.e., the constraints in ℭ\mathfrak{C} have disjoint domains), we can pick an arbitrary value λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda and define, for each v∈Vv\in V,

f⁡(v)≔{(F​(𝔠))​(v)if ​v∈𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)​ for some (unique) ​𝔠∈ℭ,λif ​v∉𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(ℭ).f(v)\,\coloneqq\,\begin{cases}\big(F(\mathfrak{c})\big)(v)&\text{if }v\in\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\text{ for some {(}unique{)} }\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C},\\ \lambda&\text{if }v\notin\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{C}).\end{cases}

Then f:V→Λf\colon V\to\Lambda is a Borel solution to Π\Pi, as desired. ∎

As mentioned in the introduction, the proof technique we employ to establish Lemma 1.17 is the method of conditional probabilities, which is essentially based on a greedy algorithm. We will construct a Borel solution to the given CSP Π\Pi in a finite number of stages. At the start of each stage, some of the variables will already have their labels determined, and our goal will be to extend this partial labeling to a larger set of variables, yielding a solution to Π\Pi in the end. We will achieve this by repeatedly applying Lemma 3.2 to certain auxiliary CSPs.

To help with the analysis of this inductive construction, we introduce the following notation. Given U⊆VU\subseteq V and f:U→Λf\colon U\to\Lambda, the quotient CSP Π/f\Pi/f encodes the problem of extending ff to a full solution to Π\Pi. That is, we define

Π/f≔(V∖U,Λ,ℭ,𝖽𝗈𝗆/f,ℬ/f),\Pi/f\,\coloneqq\,\big(V\setminus U,\,\Lambda,\,\mathfrak{C},\,\mathsf{dom}/f,\,\mathcal{B}/f\big),

where, for 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, (𝖽𝗈𝗆/f)​(𝔠)≔𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)∖U(\mathsf{dom}/f)(\mathfrak{c})\coloneqq\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\setminus U and (ℬ/f)​(𝔠)(\mathcal{B}/f)(\mathfrak{c}) is the set of all labelings φ∈Λ𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)∖U\varphi\in\Lambda^{\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\setminus U} such that extending ff by φ\varphi would violate 𝔠\mathfrak{c}. In other words, for all φ:(𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)∖U)→Λ\varphi\colon(\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\setminus U)\to\Lambda, we have

φ∈(ℬ/f)(𝔠)⟺f|𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)∩U∪φ∈ℬ(𝔠).\varphi\,\in\,(\mathcal{B}/f)(\mathfrak{c})\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad{{f}|_{\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\cap U}}\,\cup\,\varphi\,\in\,\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c}).

By definition, f′:(V∖U)→Λf^{\prime}\colon(V\setminus U)\to\Lambda is a solution to Π/f\Pi/f if and only if f∪f′f\cup f^{\prime} is a solution to Π\Pi. Let us now make a few observations:

  1. (i)

    It is possible that 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)⊆U\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\subseteq U for some 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}. In this case, (𝖽𝗈𝗆/f)​(𝔠)=∅(\mathsf{dom}/f)(\mathfrak{c})=\varnothing and (ℬ/f)​(𝔠)(\mathcal{B}/f)(\mathfrak{c}) is equal to ∅\varnothing if ff satisfies 𝔠\mathfrak{c} and {∅}\{\varnothing\} if ff violates 𝔠\mathfrak{c} (in the CSP Π\Pi).

  2. (ii)

    Since (𝖽𝗈𝗆/f)​(𝔠)⊆𝖽𝗈𝗆​(𝔠)(\mathsf{dom}/f)(\mathfrak{c})\subseteq\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c}) for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, the dependency graph of Π/f\Pi/f is a subgraph of DD. In particular, its maximum degree is at most that of Π\Pi.

  3. (iii)

    If UU is a Borel subset of VV and ff is a Borel function, then Π/f\Pi/f is a Borel CSP.

We can now describe the inductive step in the proof of Lemma 1.17. For a graph GG and r∈ℕr\in{\mathbb{N}}, let GrG^{r} be the graph with V⁡(Gr)≔V⁡(G)V(G^{r})\coloneqq V(G) and E⁡(Gr)≔{{x,y}∈[V⁡(G)]2:y∈BG​(x,r)}E(G^{r})\coloneqq\{\{x,y\}\in[V(G)]^{2}\,:\,y\in B_{G}(x,r)\}.

Lemma 3.3.

Suppose the maximum degree of DD is at most d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}}. If ℑ⊆ℭ\mathfrak{I}\subseteq\mathfrak{C} is a Borel D2D^{2}-independent set, then there is a Borel function f:𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(ℑ)→Λf\colon\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{I})\to\Lambda such that for all 𝔞∈ℭ\mathfrak{a}\in\mathfrak{C},

(3.4) ℙ⁡[(ℬ/f)​(𝔞)]⩽{(d+1)​ℙ​[ℬ⁡(𝔞)]if ​𝔞∈N⁡[ℑ],ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔞)]if ​𝔞∉N⁡[ℑ].\mathbb{P}[(\mathcal{B}/f)(\mathfrak{a})]\,\leqslant\,\begin{cases}(d+1)\,\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a})]&\text{if }\mathfrak{a}\in N[\mathfrak{I}],\\ \mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a})]&\text{if }\mathfrak{a}\notin N[\mathfrak{I}].\end{cases}
Proof.

Form an auxiliary CSP Π′\Pi^{\prime} as follows:

Π′≔(𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(ℑ),Λ,ℑ,𝖽𝗈𝗆|ℑ,𝒜),\Pi^{\prime}\,\coloneqq\,\big(\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{I}),\,\Lambda,\,\mathfrak{I},\,{{\mathsf{dom}}|_{\mathfrak{I}}},\,\mathcal{A}\big),

where for each 𝔠∈ℑ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{I}, 𝒜⁡(𝔠)\mathcal{A}(\mathfrak{c}) is the set of all mappings φ:𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)→Λ\varphi\colon\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})\to\Lambda such that

ℙ⁡[(ℬ/φ)​(𝔞)]>(d+1)​ℙ​[ℬ⁡(𝔞)]for some ​𝔞∈N⁡[𝔠].\mathbb{P}[(\mathcal{B}/\varphi)(\mathfrak{a})]\,>\,(d+1)\,\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a})]\quad\text{for some }\mathfrak{a}\in N[\mathfrak{c}].

Note that the set

Q≔{(𝔠,φ,𝔞)∈ℑ×[V⇢Λ]<∞×ℭ:φ∈Λ𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠) and ℙ[(ℬ/φ)(𝔞)]>(d+1)ℙ[ℬ(𝔞)]}Q\,\coloneqq\,\big\{(\mathfrak{c},\varphi,\mathfrak{a})\in\mathfrak{I}\times[{V}\dashrightarrow{\Lambda}]^{<\infty}\times\mathfrak{C}\,:\,\varphi\in\Lambda^{\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})}\text{ and }\mathbb{P}[(\mathcal{B}/\varphi)(\mathfrak{a})]>(d+1)\,\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a})]\big\}

is Borel by [32, Thm. 17.25]. Therefore, the set

{(𝔠,φ)∈ℑ×[V⇢Λ]<∞:φ∈𝒜(𝔠)}={(𝔠,φ):∃𝔞∈N[𝔠]((𝔠,φ,𝔞)∈Q)}\displaystyle\big\{(\mathfrak{c},\varphi)\in\mathfrak{I}\times[{V}\dashrightarrow{\Lambda}]^{<\infty}\,:\,\varphi\in\mathcal{A}(\mathfrak{c})\big\}\,=\,\big\{(\mathfrak{c},\varphi)\,:\,\exists\mathfrak{a}\in N[\mathfrak{c}]\,\big((\mathfrak{c},\varphi,\mathfrak{a})\in Q\big)\big\}

is also Borel by the Luzin–Novikov theorem [32, Thm. 18.10]. It follows that Π′\Pi^{\prime} is a Borel CSP.

Since ℑ\mathfrak{I} is D2D^{2}-independent, the constraints in ℑ\mathfrak{I} have disjoint domains, so the dependency graph of Π′\Pi^{\prime} has no edges. Next we argue that ℙ⁡[𝒜⁡(𝔠)]<1\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{A}(\mathfrak{c})]<1 for all 𝔠∈ℑ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{I}. For 𝔞∈N⁡[𝔠]\mathfrak{a}\in N[\mathfrak{c}] and φ∈Λ𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)\varphi\in\Lambda^{\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})}, let

X𝔞​(φ)≔ℙ⁡[(ℬ/φ)​(𝔞)].X_{\mathfrak{a}}(\varphi)\,\coloneqq\,\mathbb{P}[(\mathcal{B}/\varphi)(\mathfrak{a})].

By Fubini’s theorem, the expectation of the random variable X𝔞​(φ)X_{\mathfrak{a}}(\varphi) with respect to a random choice of φ∼ℙ𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)\varphi\sim\mathbb{P}^{\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})} is 𝔼⁡[X𝔞​(φ)]=ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔞)]\mathbb{E}[X_{\mathfrak{a}}(\varphi)]=\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a})]. If ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔞)]=0\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a})]=0, then X𝔞​(φ)=0X_{\mathfrak{a}}(\varphi)=0 almost surely. On the other hand, if ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔞)]>0\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a})]>0, then, by Markov’s inequality,

ℙ[X𝔞(φ)>(d+1)ℙ[ℬ(𝔞)]]<𝔼​[X𝔞​(φ)](d+1)​ℙ​[ℬ⁡(𝔞)]=1d+1.\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\big[X_{\mathfrak{a}}(\varphi)>(d+1)\,\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a})]\big]\,<\,\frac{\mathbb{E}[X_{\mathfrak{a}}(\varphi)]}{(d+1)\,\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a})]}\,=\,\frac{1}{d+1}.

Therefore, regardless of the value of ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔞)]\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a})], the union bound gives

ℙ[𝒜(𝔠)]⩽∑𝔞∈N⁡[𝔠]ℙ[X𝔞(φ)>(d+1)ℙ[ℬ(𝔞)]]<1d+1⋅|N[𝔠]|⩽ 1.\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{A}(\mathfrak{c})]\,\leqslant\,\sum_{\mathfrak{a}\in N[\mathfrak{c}]}\mathbb{P}\big[X_{\mathfrak{a}}(\varphi)>(d+1)\,\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a})]\big]\,<\,\frac{1}{d+1}\cdot|N[\mathfrak{c}]|\,\leqslant\,1.

It follows that Π′\Pi^{\prime} has a Borel solution f:𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(ℑ)→Λf\colon\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{I})\to\Lambda by Lemma 3.2. We claim that ff is as desired. Indeed, take any 𝔞∈ℭ\mathfrak{a}\in\mathfrak{C}. We verify (3.4) for 𝔞\mathfrak{a}. If 𝔞∉N⁡[ℑ]\mathfrak{a}\notin N[\mathfrak{I}], then (ℬ/f)​(𝔞)=ℬ​(𝔞)(\mathcal{B}/f)(\mathfrak{a})=\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a}) and we are done. On the other hand, if 𝔞∈N⁡[ℑ]\mathfrak{a}\in N[\mathfrak{I}], then there is a constraint 𝔠∈ℑ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{I} with 𝔞∈N⁡[𝔠]\mathfrak{a}\in N[\mathfrak{c}], and such 𝔠\mathfrak{c} is unique because ℑ\mathfrak{I} is D2D^{2}-independent. Let φ≔f|𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(𝔠)\varphi\coloneqq{{f}|_{\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{c})}}. Then (ℬ/f)​(𝔞)=(ℬ/φ)​(𝔞)(\mathcal{B}/f)(\mathfrak{a})=(\mathcal{B}/\varphi)(\mathfrak{a}). Since ff is a solution to Π′\Pi^{\prime}, we have φ∉𝒜⁡(𝔠)\varphi\notin\mathcal{A}(\mathfrak{c}), which yields ℙ⁡[(ℬ/φ)​(𝔞)]⩽(d+1)​ℙ​[ℬ⁡(𝔞)]\mathbb{P}[(\mathcal{B}/\varphi)(\mathfrak{a})]\leqslant(d+1)\,\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a})], as claimed. ∎

Proof of Lemma 1.17.

Suppose p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1) and d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}} are such that ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔠)]⩽p\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})]\leqslant p for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C}, the maximum degree of DD is at most dd, and p​(d+1)d+1<1p\,(d+1)^{d+1}<1. We seek a Borel solution to Π\Pi.

Note that the maximum degree of D2D^{2} is at most d2d^{2}. Hence, by [31, Prop. 4.6], there is a partition ℭ=ℑ1∪…∪ℑn\mathfrak{C}=\mathfrak{I}_{1}\cup\ldots\cup\mathfrak{I}_{n} of ℭ\mathfrak{C} into n⩽d2+1n\leqslant d^{2}+1 Borel D2D^{2}-independent sets. Let

Ui≔𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(ℑi)∖(𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(ℑ1)∪…∪𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(ℑi−1)).U_{i}\,\coloneqq\,\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{I}_{i})\setminus(\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{I}_{1})\cup\ldots\cup\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{I}_{i-1})).

Applying Lemma 3.3 iteratively, we obtain a sequence of Borel labelings fi:Ui→Λf_{i}\colon U_{i}\to\Lambda such that for all 𝔞∈ℭ\mathfrak{a}\in\mathfrak{C} and 1⩽i⩽n1\leqslant i\leqslant n,

ℙ⁡[(ℬ/(f1∪…∪fi))​(𝔞)]⩽{(d+1)​ℙ​[(ℬ/(f1∪…∪fi−1))​(𝔞)]if ​𝔞∈N⁡[ℑi],ℙ⁡[(ℬ/(f1∪…∪fi−1))​(𝔞)]if ​𝔞∉N⁡[ℑi].\mathbb{P}[(\mathcal{B}/(f_{1}\cup\ldots\cup f_{i}))(\mathfrak{a})]\,\leqslant\,\begin{cases}(d+1)\,\mathbb{P}[(\mathcal{B}/(f_{1}\cup\ldots\cup f_{i-1}))(\mathfrak{a})]&\text{if }\mathfrak{a}\in N[\mathfrak{I}_{i}],\\ \mathbb{P}[(\mathcal{B}/(f_{1}\cup\ldots\cup f_{i-1}))(\mathfrak{a})]&\text{if }\mathfrak{a}\notin N[\mathfrak{I}_{i}].\end{cases}

Fix any λ∈Λ\lambda\in\Lambda and define f:V→Λf\colon V\to\Lambda by

f⁡(v)≔{fi​(v)if ​v∈Ui​ for some 1⩽i⩽n,λif ​v∉𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(ℭ).f(v)\,\coloneqq\,\begin{cases}f_{i}(v)&\text{if }v\in U_{i}\text{ for some $1\leqslant i\leqslant n$},\\ \lambda&\text{if }v\notin\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{C}).\end{cases}

Since for each constraint 𝔞∈ℭ\mathfrak{a}\in\mathfrak{C}, there are |N⁡[𝔞]||N[\mathfrak{a}]| indices 1⩽i⩽n1\leqslant i\leqslant n with 𝔞∈N⁡[ℑi]\mathfrak{a}\in N[\mathfrak{I}_{i}], we have

ℙ⁡[(ℬ/f)​(𝔞)]=ℙ⁡[(ℬ/(f1∪…∪fn))​(𝔞)]⩽(d+1)|N⁡[𝔞]|​ℙ​[ℬ⁡(𝔞)]⩽(d+1)d+1​p< 1.\mathbb{P}[(\mathcal{B}/f)(\mathfrak{a})]\,=\,\mathbb{P}[(\mathcal{B}/(f_{1}\cup\ldots\cup f_{n}))(\mathfrak{a})]\,\leqslant\,(d+1)^{|N[\mathfrak{a}]|}\,\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{a})]\,\leqslant\,(d+1)^{d+1}\,p\,<\,1.

But ff is defined on all of VV, so (𝖽𝗈𝗆/f)​(𝔞)=∅(\mathsf{dom}/f)(\mathfrak{a})=\varnothing, i.e., (ℬ/f)​(𝔞)(\mathcal{B}/f)(\mathfrak{a}) is either ∅\varnothing or {∅}\{\varnothing\}. The latter case is impossible as ℙ⁡[{∅}]=1\mathbb{P}[\{\varnothing\}]=1, hence (ℬ/f)​(𝔞)=∅(\mathcal{B}/f)(\mathfrak{a})=\varnothing. This means that ff satisfies 𝔞\mathfrak{a}. Therefore, ff is a Borel solution to Π\Pi, and the proof is complete. ∎

3.3.  Proof of Theorem 1.15

Recall the set-up of Theorem 1.15: We have parameters p∈[0,1)p\in[0,1), d∈ℕd\in{\mathbb{N}}, and s>1s>1 such that:

  1. (i)

    ℙ⁡[ℬ⁡(𝔠)]⩽p\mathbb{P}[\mathcal{B}(\mathfrak{c})]\leqslant p for all 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} and the maximum degree of DD is at most dd,

  2. (ii)

    𝖾𝗀𝗋⁡(D)<s\mathsf{egr}(D)<s, and

  3. (iii)

    p​(𝖾⁡(d+1))s<1p\,(\mathsf{e}\,(d+1))^{s}<1.

Our goal is to find a Borel solution to Π\Pi.

We start by observing that the Moser–Tardos Algorithm can be used in the Borel setting:

Claim 3.5.

If τ:V→Λℕ\tau\colon V\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}} is a Borel good table, then Π\Pi has a Borel solution f∈𝖬𝖬𝖳𝖠⁡(Π,τ)f\in\mathsf{MMTA}(\Pi,\tau).

Proof.

It is enough to argue that there is a Borel function f∈𝖬𝖬𝖳𝖠⁡(Π,τ)f\in\mathsf{MMTA}(\Pi,\tau), since such ff would be defined on all of VV because τ\tau is good, and hence be a solution to Π\Pi by Lemma 2.3. To this end, we observe that if Π\Pi and τ\tau are Borel, then the Maximal Moser–Tardos Algorithm can be carried out on input (Π,τ)(\Pi,\tau) so that all of ℓn\ell_{n}, fnf_{n}, ℭn\mathfrak{C}_{n}, ℑn\mathfrak{I}_{n}, ℓ\ell, ff are Borel. Indeed, ℓ0\ell_{0} is Borel because so is τ\tau. If ℓn\ell_{n} is Borel, then so is fnf_{n}, and ℭn\mathfrak{C}_{n} is Borel as well because Π\Pi is Borel. We can then choose a Borel maximal DD-independent subset ℑn⊆ℭn\mathfrak{I}_{n}\subseteq\mathfrak{C}_{n} using [31, Prop. 4.2]. The set 𝖽𝗈𝗆⁡(ℑn)\mathsf{dom}(\mathfrak{I}_{n}) is also Borel, and thus ℓn+1\ell_{n+1} is Borel as well. Finally, if ℓn\ell_{n} is Borel for all n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}, then ℓ\ell and ff are also Borel. ∎

Next we show that the CSP 𝖫𝖦⁡(R,N,ε)\mathsf{LG}(R,N,\varepsilon) defined in §2.2 (specifically in Lemma 2.9) is Borel:

Claim 3.6.

For each RR, N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}} and ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), the CSP 𝖫𝖦⁡(R,N,ε)\mathsf{LG}(R,N,\varepsilon) is Borel.

Proof.

The function 𝖽𝗈𝗆R:ℭ→[V]<∞\mathsf{dom}_{R}\colon\mathfrak{C}\to[V]^{<\infty} is Borel by the Luzin–Novikov theorem [32, Thm. 18.10], see [39, Corl. 5.2] for details. To see that the set Q≔{(𝔠,φ)∈ℭ×[V⇢Λℕ]<∞:φ∈ℒR,N,ε(𝔠)}Q\coloneqq\{(\mathfrak{c},\varphi)\in\mathfrak{C}\times[{V}\dashrightarrow{\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}}}]^{<\infty}\,:\,\varphi\in\mathcal{L}_{R,N,\varepsilon}(\mathfrak{c})\} is Borel, we use the characterization of (𝔠,R,N,ε)(\mathfrak{c},R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good tables from Lemma 2.13, which shows that, as there are only countably many (𝔠,R)(\mathfrak{c},R)-bounded finite 𝖬𝖳\mathsf{MT}-sequences for each 𝔠∈ℭ\mathfrak{c}\in\mathfrak{C} and R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}}, QQ is also Borel by the Luzin–Novikov theorem [32, Thm. 18.10]. ∎

Take ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1) such that 𝖾𝗀𝗋⁡(D)<(1−ε)−1<s\mathsf{egr}(D)<(1-\varepsilon)^{-1}<s. By the definition of the exponential growth rate, there is R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}} such that γD​(R)<(1−ε)−R\gamma_{D}(R)<(1-\varepsilon)^{-R}. On the other hand, the inequality (1−ε)−1<s(1-\varepsilon)^{-1}<s is equivalent to ε+1/s<1\varepsilon+1/s<1, and we can take η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1) so small that

1−η1+η>p1−ε−1s.\frac{1-\eta}{1+\eta}\,>\,p^{1-\varepsilon-\frac{1}{s}}.

Finally, we take N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}} so large that

(1+η)N>F⁡(d,η,R)​γD​(2​R+1)γD​(2​R+1),(1+\eta)^{N}\,>\,F(d,\eta,R)\,\gamma_{D}(2R+1)^{\gamma_{D}(2R+1)},

where F⁡(d,η,R)F(d,\eta,R) is the function from Lemma 2.11. Claim 3.6 and Lemmas 2.10 and 2.11 imply that the CSP 𝖫𝖦⁡(R,N,ε)\mathsf{LG}(R,N,\varepsilon) satisfies the assumptions of Lemma 1.17. Therefore, 𝖫𝖦⁡(R,N,ε)\mathsf{LG}(R,N,\varepsilon) has a Borel solution τ:V→Λℕ\tau\colon V\to\Lambda^{\mathbb{N}}. In other words, τ\tau is a Borel (R,N,ε)(R,N,\varepsilon)-locally good table. By Lemma 2.8, τ\tau is good, so, by Claim 3.5, there exists a Borel solution to Π\Pi, and we are done.
